Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma in a 34-year-old Navy Officer, 'Known People: Related people' is hard to reconcile as a trauma-linked trigger without any accompanying memory or appraisal content about bereavement, loss of specific others, or interpersonal aspects of the disaster. The rest of the profile does not explain why related people would be a salient trigger.

issues.item: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Evaluation' is poorly matched to the rest of the profile. It suggests social/performance shame concerns, but the negative appraisals and memory items do not involve appearance, performance failure, humiliation, or social judgment. This maladaptive strategy appears to address a symptom theme not otherwise represented.

'Avoid Friends' similarly implies socially driven withdrawal, yet the selected appraisals are global despair and alienation rather than fear of specific interpersonal consequences, and the trigger set does not include friendship or social contact themes. It is not impossible, but in combination with 'Avoid Evaluation' it pulls toward a social-evaluative formulation not supported elsewhere.

For a natural-disaster trauma in a Navy officer, 'Similar cars' is hard to connect clinically to the rest of the profile. The other triggers are generic situational reminders (crowding, locations), but this item implies a specific vehicle-related cue that is not supported by the trauma type, memory content, or appraisals.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: The negative appraisals are extremely global and severe ('life not worth living', 'belong nowhere') relative to the rest of the selected items, which focus on trauma reminders, fragmented imagery, and avoidance. This creates a coherence problem because the profile lacks corresponding threat content or broader self-concept material to support such pervasive suicidal/existential beliefs.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: 'I no longer belong anywhere' is especially difficult to reconcile with the demographic/contextual profile of a married Navy officer after a natural disaster unless other items indicate moral injury, social alienation, or occupational rupture; none are present in the selected components.

vignette:
James Keller still remembers the moment the lights went out. It was during the second night of Hurricane Mariana, when his destroyer had been fighting the sea for hours. He was in the officers' mess, a cramped compartment below the waterline, with twenty other men packed shoulder to shoulder when the ship took a wave that threw everything sideways. The emergency lights failed, and the space went pitch black. He heard the crash of bottles breaking behind the bar-the sharp, sweet smell of rum filling the hot, wet air as seawater began seeping under the door. In the chaos he found himself wedged against a bulkhead, knees drawn up, hands pressed flat against the deck, certain the ship was going to roll and never come back. They were trapped in the dark for what felt like an hour before the damage control team got them out.

Now, more than a year later, James cannot walk into a room that is windowless without feeling his body lock into that same crouch. His shoulders hunch, his hands go flat, and for a few seconds he is right back in that mess, waiting to die. The memories come mostly as images-sharp pictures of a flooded corridor, of a man's face lit by a flash of emergency torch, of the black waterline rising-so vivid that sometimes he has to shake his head to clear them. What frightens him most is how unreal the whole event feels. He knows it happened, he carries it in his body, yet part of his mind insists it was too extreme to be real, which leaves him doubting his own history.

Crowding became unbearable almost immediately. On base, the chow hall at lunch is a gauntlet he avoids at all costs. The press of bodies, the noise, the humid air-he cannot do it. He has started eating alone in his office or skipping meals entirely. The smell of alcohol is a separate terror. Last month, at a mandatory change-of-command ceremony, a retired commander clapped him on the back, and the whiskey on the man's breath sent James into a full-body sweat, heart hammering, vision narrowing. He excused himself and did not return. His wife, Cara, has asked him to stop at the grocery store on his way home; he cannot go anywhere near the beer aisle.

He has stopped seeing his friends from the ship. Several of them called, texted, invited him to a barbecue at the beach. He could not bring himself to answer. They were there; they know what happened. Being with them would mean acknowledging it out loud, and worse, it would mean standing near a cooler full of beer. The only place he feels somewhat safe is his house, but even there, a flickering bulb in the hallway sends him into a panic because it means he might be in the dark again. He has replaced every light fixture with bright LEDs and sleeps with the bedroom door cracked open.

James has started telling himself that he deserves to suffer for what happened. He cannot articulate exactly why. No one died, though several men were injured. Yet he has become certain that his own misery is a kind of payment-a way to balance the account from that night. He used to be a happy person, quick to laugh, the kind of officer junior sailors looked up to. Now he is miserable, and he has come to believe that is simply who he is. He no longer feels he belongs anywhere. On base, he is a stranger among men who did not live through that storm. At home, Cara tries to understand, but she cannot, and the distance between them has grown until he feels set apart from everyone he once loved.

What finally brought him into the clinic was a fitness report that included the words "withdrawn" and "difficult to count on." His commanding officer told him he was being referred for evaluation. James is afraid-afraid that talking about it will make the images worse, afraid that admitting how much he avoids will get him medically separated from the only career he has known. But deeper than that, he is hoping for something he can barely name. A way to feel like he belongs to his own life again.
